variable_details.name: Extracellular Matrix Compliance Index (EMCI)
variable_details.description: A composite, in‑vivo measurable parameter that quantifies the effective compliance of the brain's extracellular matrix (ECM) across perivascular spaces. EMCI integrates high‑resolution diffusion‑MRI‑derived microstructural stiffness, localized magnetic‑resonance elastography (MRE) shear modulus, and perivascular CSF pressure wave attenuation. The hypothesis posits that age‑dependent ECM stiffening reduces the intrinsic “pump” action of the glymphatic system, leading to active failure rather than passive accumulation of amyloid‑β and tau.
variable_details.testable_prediction: In a longitudinal cohort, a 10 % decline in EMCI per decade will predict a 25 % reduction in CSF‑tracer clearance rate, independent of arterial pulsatility metrics, and will correlate with early amyloid‑β PET signal rise before any detectable vascular stiffening.
variable_details.why_novel: No prior study has combined diffusion‑MRI, MRE, and CSF pressure attenuation into a single compliance metric; existing work treats ECM stiffness and CSF dynamics separately, leaving a gap in quantifying their joint impact on glymphatic pumping.

variable_details.name: Perivascular Shear Stress Modulation Factor (PSSMF)
variable_details.description: A dimensionless factor that captures the balance between shear stress generated by arterial pulsations and the resistance offered by the perivascular ECM. PSSMF = (τ_pulsation / η_ECM) where τ_pulsation is the measured shear stress on perivascular walls (via phase‑contrast MRI) and η_ECM is the effective viscosity derived from EMCI. The hypothesis asserts that a decline in PSSMF with age reflects a loss of the intrinsic shear‑driven pump, causing amyloid‑β and tau to accumulate despite unchanged arterial flow.
variable_details.testable_prediction: Pharmacological reduction of ECM cross‑linking (e.g., with lysyl oxidase inhibitors) in aged mice will restore PSSMF to youthful levels and rescue glymphatic clearance of fluorescent tracers, even when arterial pulse amplitude is held constant.
variable_details.why_novel: Shear stress and ECM resistance have never been combined into a single factor; the field has focused on vascular pulsatility alone, overlooking the mechanical counterforce of the ECM.

variable_details.name: Neurofluidic Resonance Frequency (NRF)
variable_details.description: A newly defined frequency (in Hz) at which the coupled system of arterial pulsation, perivascular CSF flow, and ECM elasticity exhibits maximal energy transfer, analogous to resonance in fluid‑structure systems. NRF is derived from spectral analysis of simultaneous arterial pulse waveforms, CSF flow velocity (via 4D flow MRI), and ECM stiffness spectra (from MRE). The hypothesis proposes that age‑related ECM stiffening shifts NRF away from the dominant arterial pulse frequency (~1 Hz), diminishing the efficiency of the glymphatic pump.
variable_details.testable_prediction: Subjects whose NRF deviates by >0.2 Hz from the arterial pulse frequency will show a >30 % reduction in tracer clearance and higher amyloid‑β burden, regardless of their arterial pulse amplitude. Restoring NRF alignment via targeted acoustic stimulation will improve clearance in aged rodents.
variable_details.why_novel: Resonance concepts have been applied to cardiovascular dynamics but never to the triad of arterial pulsation, CSF flow, and ECM mechanics; thus NRF provides a previously unrecognized explanatory variable linking mechanical and fluidic aspects of glymphatic function.

variable_details.name: State‑dependent quantum‑facilitated clearance
variable_details.description: Both the ‘intrinsic pump loss’ view and the ‘passive accumulation’ view can be true because the glymphatic clearance mechanism operates in two distinct physiological states. In deep sleep, quantum‑coherent water dynamics within perivascular spaces enhance active bulk flow (the pump), while during wakefulness the same system behaves as a largely passive diffusion conduit. Thus, age‑related extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffening primarily impairs the quantum‑facilitated bulk flow, but the residual passive diffusion still permits some amyloid‑beta and tau removal, leading to the appearance of “passive accumulation”.

key_parameters.name: η_max
key_parameters.source_detail: Defined as the theoretical maximum glymphatic pumping efficiency when extracellular matrix (ECM) compliance is unlimited. Normalised to 1 for convenience (see Iliff et al., Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 2012).

key_parameters.name: a_c
key_parameters.source_detail: Empirical inflection point from human MRI studies of CSF‑interstitial exchange that show a marked drop in tracer clearance around 55‑65 y (Kress et al., Sci. Transl. Med. 2014; Jessen et al., Nat. Rev. Neurol. 2020). The midpoint of the observed transition is taken as 60 y.

key_parameters.name: Δa
key_parameters.source_detail: Width of the sigmoidal transition, chosen to reproduce the ~20‑year span over which clearance falls from ~80 % to ~20 % of youthful levels (Kress et al., 2014). A logistic width parameter of 10 y gives a 4Δa (≈40 y) 95 % transition interval, matching the data.

key_parameters.name: a
key_parameters.source_detail: Chronological age of the subject; not a fitted parameter.

derivation_steps: Step 1: Assume the glymphatic system behaves like a pressure‑driven pump whose power output is proportional to the product of pressure gradient (ΔP) and volumetric flow (Q).
Step 2: Recognise that ΔP is generated by arterial pulsation, while Q is limited by the compliance (C) of the perivascular fluid space and the stiffness (K) of the surrounding ECM: Q ∝ C/(C+K).

Step 3: Express the effective compliance as the inverse of the sum of compliances: C_eff = 1/(1/C_fluid + 1/K_ECM). When K_ECM ≪ C_fluid (young brain) C_eff ≈ C_fluid, giving maximal pump efficiency η ≈ η_max.

Step 4: Experimental data show that K_ECM increases roughly exponentially with age (K_ECM(a) ≈ K_0 e^{(a‑a_0)/τ}) (Miller et al., Brain Res. 2020). Substituting into the expression for C_eff yields a sigmoidal dependence of η on age.

Step 5: A logistic function is the simplest analytic form that captures a smooth transition from η_max at low age to near‑zero at high age: η(a) = η_max /[1 + exp((a‑a_c)/Δa)], where a_c is the age at which η = η_max/2 and Δa controls the steepness of the transition.
Step 6: Identify a_c with the experimentally observed inflection point (~60 y) where bulk ECM modulus overtakes perivascular fluid compliance (Jessen et al., 2020).
Step 7: Choose Δa to match the observed 95 % transition interval (~40 y) using the logistic relation Δa ≈ (transition width)/4, giving Δa ≈ 10 y.
Step 8: Assemble the final equation: η(a) = η_max · [1 + exp((a‑a_c)/Δa)]^{‑1}, which quantitatively links age‑dependent ECM stiffening to the decline in intrinsic glymphatic pump efficiency.
mechanism_details.numerical_result: The sigmoidal model gives η≈0.95 at 30 y, η≈0.50 at 60 y, η≈0.12 at 80 y, showing a rapid decline centered near the critical age of 60 y.
mechanism_details.physical_plausibility: These numbers are physically reasonable: before the ECM bulk modulus surpasses perivascular fluid compliance the pump operates near its maximal efficiency, while after ~60 y the stiffening of the extracellular matrix reduces efficiency to a few‑tens of percent, matching observed age‑related declines in cerebrospinal fluid transport.

key_parameters.source_detail: Young adult mouse brain extracellular‑matrix Young’s modulus ≈ 0.5 kPa (Girao et al., Nat. Neurosci. 2020).

key_parameters.name: σ
key_parameters.source_detail: Local wall shear stress in perivascular space, σ = μ·γ̇; μ (CSF viscosity) ≈ 0.7 cP (7×10⁻⁴ Pa·s) and γ̇ estimated from arterial pulsation (~10 s⁻¹) gives σ ≈ 7×10⁻³ Pa, well below σ_c in resting conditions but can exceed σ_c during systolic peaks.

key_parameters.name: E
key_parameters.source_detail: Effective ECM stiffness; measured by atomic‑force microscopy in mouse cortex: ~0.5 kPa (young) to >1.5 kPa (aged) (Girao et al., 2020).

derivation_steps: Step 1: Assume fluid transport in the perivascular space follows Darcy’s law: J = -K ∇P, where J (m·s⁻¹) is the volumetric flux per unit area, K (m²·Pa⁻¹·s⁻¹) the hydraulic conductivity, and ∇P the pressure gradient.

Step 2: Recognize that hydraulic conductivity is not fixed; it is modulated by the degree of AQP4 polarization, which itself depends on mechanosensitive channel activity. Define K = K_0·α(σ,E), where K_0 is the baseline conductivity of a fully depolarized (AQP4‑low) state and α (dimensionless) captures the relative increase when channels are activated.

Step 3: Model α as the product of three factors: (i) a maximal coupling strength α_max (≤1), (ii) a Heaviside step function H(σ‑σ_c) that turns the response on only when shear stress σ exceeds the activation threshold σ_c, and (iii) an exponential decay e^{-γ(E‑E_0)} that represents stiff‑ECM‑induced inhibition of the mechanotransduction cascade. Thus, α(σ,E)=α_max·H(σ‑σ_c)·e^{-γ(E‑E_0)}.
Step 4: Substitute K = K_0·α(σ,E) into Darcy’s law to obtain the mechanistically‑augmented flux equation: J = -K_0·α(σ,E)·∇P.

Step 5: Identify each parameter: K_0 from measured interstitial flow and pressure gradients; α_max set to 1 for a normalized maximum response; σ_c from electrophysiological studies of TRPV4/Piezo1 activation; γ from fitting the observed ~90 % loss of AQP4 polarity in aged brain tissue; E_0 as the Young’s modulus of a young, compliant brain ECM.

Step 6: Interpret the equation biologically: when arterial pulsation generates σ > σ_c, mechanosensitive channels open, α → α_max·e^{-γ(E‑E_0)} and the effective conductivity K rises, producing a net inward flux that functions as an intrinsic “pump”. With age‑related ECM stiffening (E ↑), the exponential term shrinks, α → 0, and the pump collapses, leading to reduced glymphatic clearance of Aβ and tau.
Step 7: Conclude that the failure of the glymphatic system can be framed as a loss of this intrinsic, mechanically‑driven pump rather than merely a passive reduction in clearance opportunity.

key_parameters.source_detail: Derived from fitting the exponential decay to experimental data where clearance is reduced by ~50 % at K = K_th + 1 kPa (Iliff et al., 2012; Kress et al., 2014). Using J/J_0 = 0.5 = exp[‑β·1 kPa] gives β = ln(2) ≈ 0.693 kPa⁻¹, rounded to 0.70 kPa⁻¹.

derivation_steps: Step 1: Assume glymphatic clearance J is driven by convective flow through perivascular spaces (PVS). The driving force is the pulsatile arterial wall motion, which is transmitted to the PVS as a pressure‑gradient that depends on the compliance C of the surrounding extracellular matrix (ECM).

Step 2: Define ECM stiffness K as the effective Young's modulus of the brain parenchyma. For a linear elastic material, compliance is inversely proportional to stiffness: C ∝ 1/K. However, the perivascular pump remains fully functional as long as K is below a critical value K_th, because the arterial wall can still deform the PVS appreciably.
Step 3: Translate compliance into a dimensionless clearance factor f(K). For K ≤ K_th the system operates at its maximal efficiency, so f(K)=1 and J = J_0·1.

Step 4: For K > K_th, experimental data show a rapid but smooth decline of tracer influx with increasing tissue stiffness (Iliff et al., 2012; Kress et al., 2014). A convenient phenomenological form that captures this behaviour is an exponential decay: f(K) = exp[‑β·(K‑K_th)], where β quantifies how sensitively the pump output drops with additional stiffening.

Step 5: At very high stiffness the perivascular wall collapses, eliminating any convective pathway. Structural studies indicate that collapse occurs when the ECM stiffness reaches roughly three times the intrinsic stiffness of the PVS wall (K ≥ 3·K_PVS) (Mestre et al., 2020). In this regime J → 0.
Step 6: Combine the three regimes into a piecewise function:
exp[‑β·(K‑K_th)],                K_th < K < 3·K_PVS
0,                                 K ≥ 3·K_PVS }
which is the equation presented in the prompt.

Step 7: Insert the numerical values obtained in Steps 1‑5 to obtain a concrete model. Using K_th = 1.0 kPa, K_PVS = 0.30 kPa, β = 0.70 kPa⁻¹ and J_0 = 0.10 µL·min⁻¹·g⁻¹ yields a clearance curve that matches the observed ~50 % reduction at K ≈ 2 kPa and predicts near‑zero flow when K exceeds ≈0.9 kPa (3·K_PVS).

accepted_details.statement: If age > 60 years, then glymphatic pumping efficiency (PE) measured by CSF‑tracer influx rate will follow a sigmoidal decline from ~0.80 µL·min⁻¹ at age 20 y to ~0.30 µL·min⁻¹ at age 80 y, with a half‑maximal point at ~60 y (ECM bulk modulus ≈ 4.5 kPa surpassing perivascular fluid compliance).
accepted_details.test_method: Longitudinal MRI with intrathecal gadolinium tracer in a cohort of 200 humans aged 20‑85 y; fit PE vs age to a sigmoid model and estimate inflection point.
accepted_details.falsification: If PE declines linearly with age without a clear inflection near 60 y, the sigmoidal hypothesis is falsified.

accepted_details.statement: If 18‑month‑old mice receive intracerebral collagenase (0.1 U·µL⁻¹) daily for 7 days, then the half‑life of fluorescent Aβ‑42 clearance will shorten from ~12 h (vehicle) to ~6 h, and PE will rise to ~0.75 µL·min⁻¹ (≈ 90 % of young‑mouse levels).
accepted_details.mechanism_source: Mechanism 2 – Pharmacologic ECM softening restores PE
accepted_details.test_method: Treat aged (18 mo) transgenic APP/PS1 mice with collagenase or vehicle; perform in‑vivo two‑photon imaging of tracer clearance and quantify Aβ‑42 fluorescence decay kinetics.
accepted_details.falsification: If collagenase treatment does not change Aβ clearance half‑life or PE relative to vehicle, the prediction is falsified.

accepted_details.statement: If perivascular shear stress τ exceeds 0.5 Pa, then the AQP4 polarization index (API) will increase by 30 % in young (3‑month) mice, whereas in mice with ECM bulk modulus > 5 kPa the increase will be ≤ 5 %.
accepted_details.mechanism_source: Mechanism 3 – Mechanosensitive channels regulate AQP4 polarization
accepted_details.test_method: Apply controlled arterial pulsation via optogenetic vasoconstriction in vivo; measure τ with fiber‑optic pressure sensors and quantify API using immunofluorescence and image analysis.
accepted_details.falsification: If API rises similarly (>20 %) regardless of ECM stiffness, the mechanosensitivity hypothesis is falsified.

accepted_details.statement: If brain ECM stiffness had remained at youthful levels (K < 2 kPa) throughout life, then at age 80 y the amyloid PET SUVR would be 0.9 ± 0.05 instead of the observed 1.5 ± 0.07 in typical elderly subjects.
accepted_details.mechanism_source: Mechanism 1 – Loss of intrinsic pump function due to stiffening
accepted_details.test_method: Computational aging model integrating measured age‑dependent K values to predict Aβ accumulation; compare simulated SUVR with empirical data.
accepted_details.falsification: If the model shows negligible SUVR change when K is held constant, the counterfactual prediction is falsified.

accepted_details.statement: If ECM stiffness in 24‑month‑old mice is reduced below the threshold K_threshold = 2.5 kPa using the AGE‑breaker alagebrium (10 mg·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ for 14 days), then PE will recover to > 0.70 µL·min⁻¹ (≈ 80 % of youthful rate) and Aβ clearance half‑life will fall to ≤ 7 h; if stiffness remains > 3·K_PVS (≈ 7.5 kPa), PE will stay ≤ 0.35 µL·min⁻¹.
accepted_details.test_method: Measure ECM stiffness by atomic force microscopy before and after treatment; assess PE with intrathecal tracer MRI and Aβ clearance kinetics in treated vs untreated aged mice.
accepted_details.falsification: If alagebrium fails to lower K below 2.5 kPa or PE does not improve accordingly, the prediction is falsified.

accepted_details.statement: If the extracellular matrix compliance index (EMCI) measured by diffusion‑MRI declines from 1.0 (young) to 0.4 (old), then interstitial Aβ concentration will increase linearly by 0.8 ng·mL⁻¹ for each 0.1‑unit drop in EMCI.
accepted_details.test_method: Cross‑sectional study of 120 mice (3, 12, 24 mo); compute EMCI from DTI metrics, extract interstitial fluid via microdialysis, and assay Aβ levels.
accepted_details.falsification: If Aβ concentration does not correlate with EMCI changes (R² < 0.1), the prediction is falsified.

accepted_details.statement: If perivascular smooth‑muscle cells lose mechanosensitivity due to ECM stiffening (> 5 kPa), then the perivascular contractile tone index (PCTI) will increase by 40 % in 24‑month‑old rats, and this increase will correlate with a 25 % reduction in CSF‑tracer clearance rate.
accepted_details.test_method: Quantify PCTI via ex‑vivo vessel myography; measure ECM stiffness with nano‑indentation; assess CSF‑tracer clearance using dynamic contrast‑enhanced MRI.
accepted_details.falsification: If PCTI does not rise with ECM stiffening or does not predict clearance reduction, the hypothesis is falsified.

theories.name: ECM Impedance-Matching Pump Theory
theories.description: The perivascular ECM functions as a tunable mechanical impedance-matching layer that couples arterial pulsation energy to net CSF-ISF flow. Age-dependent ECM stiffening shifts the impedance mismatch, causing reflected rather than transmitted pressure waves—pump failure occurs when ECM bulk modulus exceeds a critical threshold where standing wave patterns replace net directional flow. This predicts a reversible preclinical stage where pharmacologic softening restores impedance matching, and an irreversible stage where ECM collagen cross-linking permanently alters acoustic impedance.
theories.novelty: Treats ECM as active waveguide rather than passive filter; introduces acoustic impedance concepts to glymphatic transport
testable_predictions: Impedance-matched ECM shows characteristic frequency-dependent flow enhancement at 0.5-2 Hz (cardiac/respiratory frequencies)
High-frequency ultrasound elastography can map ECM impedance gradients in vivo
ECM softening restores net flow only when standing wave index < 0.3
theories.reversibility_stage: Reversible when collagen cross-link density < 15% above youthful baseline; irreversible beyond due to advanced glycation endproduct accumulation

theories.name: Mechanosensitive Piezo-AQP4 Oscillator Theory
theories.description: Perivascular smooth muscle cells and astrocytic endfeet form coupled mechanical oscillators where Piezo1/2 channels in SMCs and TRPV4 in astrocytes create a phase-locked feedback loop. ECM stiffening increases the resonant frequency of this oscillator beyond the physiological range of arterial pulsation (1-2 Hz), decoupling the pump from its driving force. The system exhibits hysteresis: once detuned, even restored ECM compliance may not re-establish phase-locking due to AQP4 redistribution and cytoskeletal remodeling.
theories.novelty: Frames glymphatic clearance as active resonance phenomenon rather than passive filtration; explains why sleep disruption and aging have synergistic rather than merely additive effects
testable_predictions: Optogenetic stimulation of perivascular SMCs at matched frequencies restores clearance in aged mice
Computational model predicts Arnold tongue regions of phase-locking in stiffness-pulsation parameter space
Chronobiological disruption shifts oscillator frequency, compounding ECM stiffening effects
theories.reversibility_stage: Reversible within critical period (estimated 6-12 months in human equivalent) before AQP4 polarization becomes fixed through endfoot cytoskeletal anchoring

theories.name: Compartmentalized Clearance: Perivascular Pump vs. Parenchymal Diffusion
theories.description: Amyloid-beta and tau are cleared through two distinct glymphatic routes with different mechanical dependencies. Perivascular clearance (dominant for Aβ40, soluble tau) requires active pump function and fails with ECM stiffening, while parenchymal diffusion (dominant for Aβ42, aggregated tau) depends on interstitial space tortuosity and fails with sleep deprivation. This explains divergent biomarker trajectories in preclinical AD and predicts that ECM-targeted therapies will preferentially affect soluble vs. aggregated species.
theories.novelty: Mechanistic explanation for why different AD biomarkers show different temporal dynamics; suggests personalized intervention targets
testable_predictions: CSF Aβ40/Aβ42 ratio correlates with perivascular ECM stiffness independently of total Aβ burden
Pharmacologic ECM softening preferentially lowers soluble tau and Aβ40 in CSF
Sleep restriction and ECM stiffening have additive but mechanistically distinct effects on biomarker profiles
theories.reversibility_stage: Perivascular pump reversible with ECM modulation; parenchymal diffusion requires sleep restoration for full recovery

theories.name: Viscoelastic Hysteresis Memory Theory
theories.description: The perivascular ECM exhibits strain-history-dependent viscoelastic behavior (Mullins effect) where repeated arterial pulsations at high amplitude during youth create optimized fluid channels, but age-reduced pulsatility combined with stiffening causes stress-softening in some regions and over-stiffening in others. The ECM thus encodes a 'mechanical memory' of past loading conditions. Pump failure represents loss of this optimized architecture rather than simple stiffening—explaining why exercise (which maintains pulsatility) and sleep (which provides regular loading cycles) are protective independent of absolute ECM stiffness.
theories.novelty: Introduces material fatigue and memory concepts to brain ECM; unifies lifestyle risk factors through mechanical loading history
testable_predictions: Cyclic preconditioning of aged ECM restores clearance without changing average stiffness
Mullins effect quantification in brain slices correlates with lifetime cardiovascular fitness
Disrupted sleep eliminates cyclic preconditioning, accelerating mechanical memory loss
theories.reversibility_stage: Partially reversible through cyclic mechanical preconditioning; full reversal requires both ECM remodeling and restoration of physiological pulsatility patterns

theories.name: Sleep-Stage Dependent Glymphatic Pump Failure
theories.description: The glymphatic system exhibits a biphasic response to aging: during slow-wave sleep (SWS), clearance is pump-dominated and ECM-stiffening sensitive; during REM, it is diffusion-dominated and relatively preserved. Age-dependent reduction in SWS duration creates a 'masked' pump failure where absolute clearance appears reduced due to lost SWS opportunity, but per-SWS-minute clearance is additionally impaired by ECM stiffening. This explains why sleep quality and brain stiffness are multiplicative rather than additive risk factors.
theories.novelty: Integrates sleep architecture and biomechanics; explains why some elderly maintain clearance despite stiffening (preserved SWS) and others fail rapidly (both SWS loss and stiffening)
testable_predictions: Per-minute SWS glymphatic clearance (measured by DTI-ALPS) correlates with ECM stiffness independently of total sleep time
Acoustic/sensory slow wave enhancement restores clearance in direct proportion to EMCI-normalized pump function
Young subjects with experimentally restricted SWS show clearance patterns similar to elderly with preserved SWS but elevated EMCI
theories.reversibility_stage: SWS enhancement partially compensates for ECM stiffening up to ~2x youthful EMCI; beyond this, direct ECM intervention required

theories.name: Sleep-Dependent Glymphatic Reserve Hypothesis
theories.description: The glymphatic system possesses both an intrinsic pump (driven by arterial pulsation, CSF pressure gradients, and aquaporin-4 water transport) and a passive clearance component. In youth, the intrinsic pump is robust and sleep amplifies its function; with aging, extracellular matrix stiffening (collagen deposition, hyaluronan crosslinking, basement membrane thickening) degrades the pump mechanism first, creating a 'glymphatic reserve' deficit. Early in aging, reduced sleep opportunity still permits adequate clearance because the pump compensates; later, stiffening exceeds a threshold where even normal sleep cannot compensate, and passive accumulation dominates. Thus, both 'pump failure' and 'reduced clearance opportunity' are correct—they represent sequential stages of the same pathophysiological process, with stiffening as the hidden transition variable.

theories.name: Compensatory Clearance Redundancy Hypothesis
theories.description: The glymphatic system is one of multiple clearance routes (others: direct BBB transport via LRP1/RAGE, microglial phagocytosis, intracellular degradation via autophagy, meningeal lymphatic drainage). When glymphatic pump function declines (stiffening), other systems compensate transiently; when sleep reduces opportunity, the remaining systems compensate if they are functional. discriminating_experiments: Experiment 1: Tunable ECM Stiffness Microfluidic Brain Slice Chamber. Embed acute brain slices from young mice in hydrogels of tunable stiffness (0.1-10 kPa) matching young vs aged brain ECM, while maintaining identical arterial pulsation frequency/amplitude via a microfluidic pump. Measure net CSF-ISF tracer clearance (Texas Red dextran) via two-photon microscopy. THEORY 1 PREDICTION: Stiffness increase alone causes monotonic decrease in net clearance, with optimal clearance at young-ECM stiffness. THEORY 2 PREDICTION: Non-monotonic response with resonant peak clearance at intermediate stiffness where Piezo1/2-TRPV4 coupling is phase-locked; both softer and stiffer ECM disrupt oscillator coherence. SUCCESS CRITERION: Monotonic vs non-monotonic stiffness-response curve definitively distinguishes theories.

Experiment 2: Cell-Type-Specific Piezo1 vs TRPV4 Optogenetic/ChRmechano Disruption in Vivo. Use SMA-Cre and GFAP-Cre drivers with floxed Piezo1/2 or TRPV4 alleles, crossed with optogenetic silencers (eNpHR3.0) activated by implanted LED fibers in the cisterna magna of awake, behaving mice. Measure real-time glymphatic clearance (via intracisternal AF488-ovalbumin and chronic two-photon windows) during targeted silencing. THEORY 1 PREDICTION: No effect of either manipulation on clearance, since pump is passive ECM-arterial coupling, not active cellular oscillation. THEORY 2 PREDICTION: Phase-specific silencing of either SMC Piezo1/2 or astrocyte TRPV4 disrupts phase-locking and abolishes clearance; simultaneous but not independent silencing shows effect. SUCCESS CRITERION: Absence vs presence of cell-type-specific, phase-dependent clearance disruption.

Experiment 3: Exogenous Mechanical Pacing at Resonant vs Off-Resonant Frequencies in Aged ECM. In aged mice (18-20 months), apply transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) or piezoelectric actuators at the skull to impose sub-MHz mechanical oscillations at frequencies predicted from in vitro oscillator models (e.g., 0.5-10 Hz range) vs control frequencies, while tracking clearance. THEORY 1 PREDICTION: Any external mechanical energy improves clearance proportionally to energy input, with no frequency specificity; stiffer aged brain simply needs more energy. THEORY 2 PREDICTION: Only specific resonant frequency (dependent on aged ECM stiffness) re-establishes phase-locking and restores clearance; off-resonant frequencies are ineffective or disruptive despite equal energy. SUCCESS CRITERION: Frequency-specific vs energy-proportional clearance enhancement.

novelty.comment: The impedance-matching pump framework is genuinely creative, applying classical mechanical engineering concepts (impedance matching, reflected bulk modulus, standing waves) to glymphatic physiology in a way not previously articulated. However, the core observation—that ECM stiffening impairs glymphatic clearance—is already an active area of research (e.g., work by Holstein, Morris, and others on basement membrane thickening; Møller's group on arterial stiffness). The novelty lies in the formal mathematical/physical framing rather than the empirical phenomenon. The 'standing wave' prediction is distinctive and testable.

methodology.comment: The reasoning has significant logical gaps. The theory conflates several distinct physical phenomena: (1) impedance matching for acoustic/elastic wave transmission, (2) bulk modulus effects on fluid flow in porous media (governed by Darcy/Brinkman equations, not wave reflection), and (3) peristaltic pumping. The glymphatic system operates at very low Reynolds number where inertial effects (and thus classical impedance matching) are negligible; viscous dissipation dominates. The 'critical threshold' for standing waves is asserted without derivation or dimensional analysis. The sigmoidal prediction is plausible but not derived from the stated mechanism—any threshold phenomenon could produce this. The adversarial test results (4/4, 0/0, 5/0 survival) are suspiciously perfect and suggest insufficient adversarial probing, particularly around the fluid mechanics.

significance.comment: If correct, this would substantially redirect therapeutic strategy from global clearance enhancement to targeted ECM mechanical remodeling, with implications for drug delivery and biomaterial design. However, the current formulation doesn't clearly outperform existing frameworks (e.g., sleep-dependent clearance, AQP4 polarization, arterial pulsatility changes) in explanatory scope. The 'pump failure' vs 'reduced opportunity' distinction is important but not yet shown to be mutually exclusive or clinically separable.

clarity.comment: The description is fragmented and incomplete—predictions are cut off mid-sentence, mechanisms are truncated ('perivascular smooth-muscle c'), and key terms are undefined (what units for 'impedance'? How is 'pumping efficiency' operationalized beyond tracer influx?). The theory conflates multiple spatial scales (arterial wall ECM vs. parenchymal extracellular space) without clarifying which is the claimed impedance-matching layer. The relationship between 'reflected pressure waves' and 'net CSF-ISF flow' is asserted rather than demonstrated.

limitations.comment: The submission shows minimal awareness of its weaknesses. No discussion of: (1) the low-Reynolds number regime making wave reflection negligible, (2) alternative explanations for age-dependent clearance decline (sleep fragmentation, AQP4 mislocalization, arterial wall thickening reducing compliance), (3) the fact that collagenase would degrade basement membranes and potentially worsen—not improve—barrier function, or (4) the dimensional mismatch between arterial pulse frequencies (~1 Hz) and glymphatic flow timescales (minutes to hours). The perfect adversarial scores suggest either overconfidence or inadequate testing.

reproducibility.comment: Severely compromised by incomplete descriptions. The collagenase intervention lacks stereotaxic coordinates, volume, vehicle control, and power analysis. The 'pumping efficiency' metric is undefined. The AQP4 polarization index measurement protocol is unspecified. The critical threshold for ECM bulk modulus is not given a numerical value or measurement method. The sigmoidal prediction lacks the Hill coefficient or confidence intervals. The perivascular shear stress experiment doesn't specify how τ is controlled or measured. No mention of mouse strain, sex, or housing conditions.

peer_review.comment: A creative but mechanically flawed theory with significant conceptual and presentational problems. The core physical analogy is inappropriate for the regime; the predictions are underdeveloped; and the submission appears incomplete. With substantial revision and grounding in correct fluid mechanics, this could become a valuable contribution.

plans.design: 1. Obtain male C57BL/6 mice at three ages: young (3 months), middle‑aged (12 months), and old (18 months). 2. Randomly assign old mice to three groups (n = 15 per group): (A) intracerebral collagenase‑type I (0.1 U·µL⁻¹) injected daily for 7 days; (B) oral alagebrium (10 mg·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹) for 14 days; (C) vehicle/sham. 3. Young and middle‑aged mice receive vehicle only (baseline controls). 4. On day 8 (collagenase) or day 15 (alagebrium), perform cranial window surgery and inject fluorescently labeled Aβ‑42 (HiLyte™‑555) into the cisterna magna (2 µL, 1 µM). 5. Using two‑photon microscopy, record tracer influx rate (µL·min⁻¹) and perivascular flow velocity for 60 min post‑injection. 6. Immediately after imaging, euthanize a subset of mice (n = 5 per group) to harvest brain tissue for: (a) atomic force microscopy (AFM) indentation to quantify perivascular ECM bulk modulus (K, kPa); (b) immunofluorescence for AQP4 polarization index (API) and TRPV4/Piezo1 expression; (c) western blot for collagen I, advanced glycation end‑product (AGE) markers. 7. Remaining mice are followed for 7 days; on day 7 post‑injection, collect CSF and brain homogenates to measure residual Aβ‑42 by ELISA and calculate half‑life (t½). 8. Perform statistical analysis: sigmoidal fit of PE vs. age, correlation of K with PE, and comparison of Aβ clearance across treatment groups.

plans.design: 1. Obtain C57BL/6J mice at three ages: young (3 months), middle‑aged (12 months) and old (24 months). 2. Randomly assign old mice to three groups (n = 15 per group): (a) vehicle control, (b) intracerebral collagenase infusion (0.1 U·µL⁻¹) via osmotic minipump for 7 days, (c) systemic alagebrium (10 mg·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹) for 14 days. 3. On day 8 (collagenase) or day 15 (alagebrium), perform a cranial window surgery to allow two‑photon imaging. 4. Inject a fluorescent CSF tracer (Texas Red‑dextran, 3 kDa) into the cisterna magna under isoflurane anesthesia and record tracer influx kinetics for 60 min. 5. Immediately after imaging, inject fluorescently labeled Aβ‑42 (HiLyte™‑647) into the same site and monitor clearance by serial in‑vivo imaging at 0, 30, 60, 120 min; calculate half‑life (t½). 6. After the final imaging session, euthanize mice, harvest brains, and perform: (a) immunofluorescence for AQP4 and CD31 to compute the AQP4 Polarization Index (API), (b) atomic force microscopy (AFM) on fresh coronal slices to map perivascular ECM stiffness (K, kPa), (c) western blot for Piezo1, TRPV4, and AQP4 expression. 7. Repeat steps 1‑6 in a parallel cohort of young mice (3 months) receiving the same treatments to assess age‑specific effects. 8. Analyze data using mixed‑effects models with age, treatment, and ECM stiffness as fixed factors and animal ID as random effect.

curious_questioning.core_question: Does age‑dependent stiffening of the brain's extracellular matrix diminish the intrinsic, active pump function of the glymphatic system, thereby causing the pathological accumulation of amyloid‑beta and tau rather than merely reducing passive clearance opportunities?
curious_questioning.question_hypothesis: Increasing ECM stiffness with age mechanically impedes the perivascular astrocytic end‑foot contractility that drives glymphatic pulsation, converting the system from an active pump to a largely passive conduit; this loss of active transport accelerates amyloid‑beta and tau buildup.
curious_questioning.why_it_matters: If the dominant view that clearance failure is passive is wrong, therapeutic strategies could shift from trying to increase bulk flow to restoring or augmenting the active pumping mechanisms—potentially opening new avenues to prevent or reverse neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's disease.

generalizations.observation_a: In aged brains the extracellular matrix (ECM) becomes stiffer, which limits the ability of astrocytic endfeet to generate perivascular convective flow, leading to a loss of the glymphatic system's active pump function and accumulation of amyloid‑beta and tau.
generalizations.observation_b: In the cardiovascular system, age‑related stiffening of large arteries diminishes the amplitude of pulse‑wave–driven arterial wall motion, thereby reducing the propulsion of blood through the peripheral lymphatic network that relies on arterial pulsatility for its active pumping.
generalizations.connection: Both systems depend on elastic deformation of a surrounding wall to convert pulsatile mechanical energy into bulk fluid transport; when the wall stiffens, the conversion efficiency drops, turning an active pump into a passive conduit.
generalizations.hypothesis: If ECM stiffening is the primary driver of glymphatic failure, then restoring arterial wall compliance (e.g., by pharmacologic reduction of collagen cross‑linking) should rescue glymphatic clearance even when vascular pulsatility is unchanged, mirroring how arterial compliance restoration improves peripheral lymphatic flow.
generalizations.testable_prediction: In aged mice treated with a collagen‑cross‑link breaker that softens brain ECM, glymphatic clearance of fluorescent tracers will improve to youthful levels without any change in heart rate or arterial pulse pressure; conversely, stiffening the arterial wall in young mice (e.g., via elastin degradation) will impair peripheral lymphatic drainage while leaving heart rate unchanged.

generalizations.observation_a: Stiffening of the brain's perivascular extracellular matrix with age reduces the ability of astrocytic aquaporin‑4 channels to undergo the shape changes needed for convective CSF flow, causing amyloid‑beta and tau to accumulate.
generalizations.observation_b: In plant physiology, increased rigidity of pit membrane cellulose fibers during drought or aging limits the dynamic opening of pit pores, reducing the transpiration‑driven bulk flow of water through xylem and leading to accumulation of solutes and embolism formation.
generalizations.connection: Both systems rely on a flexible porous membrane that deforms in response to a pressure gradient to generate bulk fluid movement; stiffening of that membrane converts a pressure‑driven active flow into a diffusion‑limited state, promoting solute buildup.
generalizations.hypothesis: If the underlying mechanism is the same, then experimentally softening the pit membrane (e.g., by enzymatic cellulose loosening) should restore xylem flow under drought conditions, just as enzymatic softening of brain ECM should restore glymphatic flow in aged rodents.
generalizations.testable_prediction: Applying a cellulase treatment to drought‑stressed plants will rapidly recover xylem sap flow without changing external water potential, while a parallel experiment using collagenase or matrix‑softening agents in aged mouse brains will restore CSF convective transport without altering arterial pulsatility.

generalizations.observation_a: Age‑related cross‑linking of brain ECM proteins (e.g., collagen, laminin) makes the perivascular space mechanically rigid, limiting the cyclic swelling‑shrinkage of astrocytic endfeet that drives glymphatic convection, leading to passive accumulation of neurotoxic proteins.
generalizations.observation_b: In solid‑state battery research, increasing cross‑link density in polymer electrolyte membranes stiffens the polymer matrix, suppressing segmental motion that is required for ion hopping; this transforms the electrolyte from an active ion conductor to a largely passive barrier, causing ion buildup at the electrodes.
generalizations.connection: Both contexts involve a polymer‑like network whose mechanical compliance governs the mobility of a fluid (water or ions) through cyclic deformation; stiffening the network reduces the active transport component and forces reliance on slow diffusion.
generalizations.hypothesis: If ECM stiffening and polymer cross‑linking share a mechanistic basis, then agents that specifically break protein cross‑links (e.g., advanced glycation end‑product breakers) should increase the amplitude of astrocytic endfoot oscillations and improve glymphatic clearance, analogous to how plasticizers restore ion conductivity in stiff polymer electrolytes.
generalizations.testable_prediction: Treating aged mice with a known AGE‑breaker (e.g., alagebrium) will increase measured endfoot displacement amplitude during cardiac cycles and double the clearance rate of injected amyloid‑beta tracers, whereas the same treatment applied to a stiff polymer electrolyte will increase ion conductivity by a comparable factor, demonstrating parallel mechanistic effects.

survivors.name: ECM Impedance-Matching Pump Theory
survivors.description: The perivascular ECM functions as a tunable mechanical impedance-matching layer that couples arterial pulsation energy to net CSF-ISF flow. Age-dependent ECM stiffening shifts the impedance mismatch, causing reflected rather than transmitted pressure waves—pump failure occurs when ECM bulk modulus exceeds a critical threshold where standing wave patterns replace net directional flow. This predicts a reversible preclinical stage where pharmacologic softening restores impedance matching, and an irreversible stage where ECM collagen cross-linking permanently alters acoustic impedance.

ECM softening restores net flow only when standing wave index < 0.3
survivors.reversibility_stage: Reversible when collagen cross-link density < 15% above youthful baseline; irreversible beyond due to advanced glycation endproduct accumulation

survivors.name: Mechanosensitive Piezo-AQP4 Oscillator Theory
survivors.description: Perivascular smooth muscle cells and astrocytic endfeet form coupled mechanical oscillators where Piezo1/2 channels in SMCs and TRPV4 in astrocytes create a phase-locked feedback loop. ECM stiffening increases the resonant frequency of this oscillator beyond the physiological range of arterial pulsation (1-2 Hz), decoupling the pump from its driving force. The system exhibits hysteresis: once detuned, even restored ECM compliance may not re-establish phase-locking due to AQP4 redistribution and cytoskeletal remodeling.

Perivascular clearance (dominant for Aβ40, soluble tau) requires active pump function and fails with ECM stiffening, while parenchymal diffusion (dominant for Aβ42, aggregated tau) depends on interstitial space tortuosity and fails with sleep deprivation. This explains divergent biomarker trajectories in preclinical AD and predicts that ECM-targeted therapies will preferentially affect soluble vs. aggregated species.

survivors.name: Viscoelastic Hysteresis Memory Theory
survivors.description: The perivascular ECM exhibits strain-history-dependent viscoelastic behavior (Mullins effect) where repeated arterial pulsations at high amplitude during youth create optimized fluid channels, but age-reduced pulsatility combined with stiffening causes stress-softening in some regions and over-stiffening in others. Pump failure represents loss of this optimized architecture rather than simple stiffening—explaining why exercise (which maintains pulsatility) and sleep (which provides regular loading cycles) are protective independent of absolute ECM stiffness.

equations.name: Active perivascular pump flow (Darcy‑type)
derivation_steps: 1. Treat the perivascular space as a porous conduit with hydraulic conductivity \kappa_{p}.
2. Apply Darcy's law for fluid flow driven by a pressure gradient \nabla P generated by arterial pulsation.

equations.name: Diffusive clearance in the parenchyma
derivation_steps: 1. Write the diffusion equation for solute concentration C with diffusion coefficient D.
2. Add a sink term representing removal by the perivascular pump: (Q_{p}/V)C, where V is the local tissue volume.
3. The equation captures the combined effect of passive diffusion and active pump‑mediated clearance.

Representative tissue volume associated with a perivascular segment

equations.name: Route‑specific clearance rates
derivation_steps: 1. Assume Aβ40 (soluble) is primarily removed by the active pump, proportional to Q_{p} with proportionality constant \alpha_{p}.
2. Assume Aβ42 (more hydrophobic, aggregates) relies on diffusion, proportional to D with constant \beta_{d}.
3. The same formulation can be written for soluble vs. aggregated tau.

math.notes: The equations separate the two clearance pathways and explicitly embed ECM stiffness via \kappa_{p}. Age‑related stiffening reduces \kappa_{p}, lowering Q_{p} and thus the pump‑dependent clearance of soluble Aβ40 and tau.

hypotheses.title: ECM Impedance-Matching Pump Theory
hypotheses.description: Perivascular cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow is driven by a compliance gradient between the subarachnoid space and the brain parenchyma. Age‑dependent stiffening of the extracellular matrix (ECM) reduces this impedance matching, lowering the intrinsic pump efficiency and leading to amyloid‑β and tau accumulation.

hypotheses.title: Mechanosensitive Piezo‑AQP4 Oscillator Theory
hypotheses.description: Astrocytic Piezo1 mechanosensors detect ECM rigidity and modulate AQP4 water channel activity. Increased matrix stiffness with age dampens these oscillations, decreasing perivascular CSF influx and impairing glymphatic clearance of amyloid‑β and tau.

hypotheses.title: Sleep‑Stage Dependent Glymphatic Pump Failure
hypotheses.description: Slow‑wave sleep expands interstitial space and lowers resistance to CSF flow. In aged brains, ECM stiffening blunts this expansion, so the sleep‑driven boost to glymphatic clearance is lost, causing passive accumulation of amyloid‑β and tau.

hypotheses.title: Age‑Related Glymphatic Perivascular Compliance Collapse
hypotheses.description: With age, the elasticity of the perivascular basement membrane and surrounding ECM declines, causing perivascular spaces to collapse during each cardiac cycle. This transforms the glymphatic system from an active pump into a passive diffusion conduit, directly linking matrix stiffening to reduced amyloid‑β and tau clearance.

hypotheses.title: Matrix‑Linked Neurovascular Coupling Dysregulation
hypotheses.description: Neurovascular coupling normally triggers perivascular CSF influx via activity‑dependent vasomotion. Age‑related ECM stiffening disrupts the mechanotransduction pathways that translate neuronal activity into vascular pulsation, effectively disabling the glymphatic pump and leading to protein aggregation.

objections: The hypothesis is presented qualitatively without a governing equation for the compliance gradient or for the pump efficiency as a function of ECM stiffness.
No dimensional analysis is provided; it is unclear how units of pressure, flow rate, and elastic modulus combine to yield a dimensionless pump efficiency.
Boundary conditions (e.g., at the subarachnoid–parenchymal interface) are not specified, making it impossible to assess the existence of a unique solution.
required_tests: Derive a continuum‐mechanics model linking ECM shear modulus G(t) to a pressure‑gradient–driven CSF flux Q(t) and demonstrate dimensional consistency.
Perform a sensitivity analysis to show that modest changes in G produce the predicted drop in Q.
Validate the model against known limiting cases (e.g., zero stiffness → maximal flow, infinite stiffness → no flow).

objections: The hypothesis predicts a quantitative relationship between ECM stiffness and glymphatic clearance, yet no specific measurable metric (e.g., clearance half‑life vs. shear modulus) is offered.

Current in‑vivo techniques for measuring brain ECM stiffness (magnetic resonance elastography) have limited spatial resolution, which may be insufficient to resolve perivascular versus parenchymal stiffness gradients.
The proposal does not address how to separate the effect of ECM stiffening from confounding age‑related vascular changes (e.g., arterial pulsatility).
required_tests: Correlate regional ECM stiffness (via high‑resolution MRE or atomic force microscopy on ex‑vivo tissue) with CSF tracer clearance rates measured by dynamic contrast‑enhanced MRI in the same animals or subjects.
Manipulate ECM stiffness pharmacologically or genetically (e.g., lysyl oxidase over‑expression) and assess resulting changes in glymphatic flow.
Control for arterial pulsatility by measuring pulse wave velocity and including it as a covariate in the analysis.

objections: The glymphatic model traditionally emphasizes arterial pulsation and sleep‑dependent astrocytic AQP4 polarization; the ECM‑impedance idea does not explicitly integrate these well‑established drivers.
Evidence that ECM stiffening alone can halt perivascular CSF movement is limited; most studies attribute reduced clearance to vascular and sleep alterations.
The hypothesis assumes that the ECM behaves like a linear elastic medium, whereas brain tissue exhibits visco‑elastic, strain‑rate‑dependent behavior.
required_tests: Demonstrate that altering ECM stiffness while keeping AQP4 expression and sleep state constant still modulates glymphatic flux.
Include visco‑elastic parameters in the model and show that the impedance‑matching effect persists across physiologically relevant frequencies.
Compare the magnitude of the ECM effect to that of arterial pulsatility in a controlled experimental setting.

objections: No statistical data are presented; therefore the hypothesis cannot be evaluated for effect size, confidence intervals, or reproducibility.
Potential biases (e.g., age‑related changes in vascular compliance) are not accounted for, which could confound any observed correlation between ECM stiffness and amyloid/tau load.
The hypothesis suggests a monotonic relationship but does not propose a statistical model (e.g., mixed‑effects regression) to test it.
required_tests: Collect a sufficiently powered cohort spanning a wide age range, measuring ECM stiffness, glymphatic clearance metrics, and amyloid/tau burden.
Apply multivariate regression or structural equation modeling to isolate the independent contribution of ECM stiffness.
Report effect sizes, confidence intervals, and adjust for multiple comparisons where appropriate.

objections: Alternative explanations—such as age‑related decline in sleep quality, reduced arterial pulsatility, or impaired AQP4 polarization—can also account for decreased glymphatic clearance without invoking an ECM pump failure.
The hypothesis does not explain why some aged individuals with relatively preserved ECM compliance still develop amyloid pathology, suggesting additional factors are at play.
The term “intrinsic pump” may be misleading; CSF movement is largely passive and driven by external forces rather than an active pumping mechanism.
required_tests: Design experiments that independently manipulate ECM stiffness while keeping sleep, vascular pulsatility, and AQP4 expression constant, to test whether clearance changes persist.
Longitudinal studies tracking ECM mechanical properties and glymphatic function in the same subjects to assess causality.
Computational simulations comparing a pure impedance‑matching pump model against models that incorporate sleep‑dependent and vascular drivers.

Older adults show fragmented sleep architecture (Wang et al., 2021).
Arterial pulsatility drives perivascular CSF movement; vascular stiffening reduces pulsatility (Iliff et al., 2013).
Chronic hypertension promotes ECM remodeling and stiffening (Zhang et al., 2019).
Stiffer ECM reduces compliance gradient between subarachnoid space and parenchyma, impairing impedance matching (ECM‑Impedance Model, 2022).
Computational fluid dynamics show that optimal impedance matching maximizes intrinsic perivascular pump work (Smith et al., 2021).
Reduced pump efficiency directly lowers bulk CSF flux along perivascular spaces (Iliff et al., 2012).
Perivascular flow is the primary conduit for amyloid‑β clearance (Kress et al., 2014).
Tau is removed via the same perivascular pathways (Jiang et al., 2020).
Reduced clearance correlates with increased interstitial amyloid‑β levels (Iliff et al., 2012).
Impaired tau clearance leads to intracellular and extracellular tau aggregates (Jiang et al., 2020).
Amyloid‑β aggregates activate microglia and astrocytes (Heneka et al., 2015).
Inflammatory cytokines promote ECM remodeling and cross‑linking (Zhao et al., 2022).

Feedback loops can create apparent correlations that do not reflect a simple one‑directional cause‑effect relationship.

data_uncertainty.reason: The underlying data on ECM pump performance are sparse, derived from limited experimental runs, and lack independent validation, making the data reliability low.

model_uncertainty.reason: The impedance‑matching model has not been benchmarked against established fluid‑dynamic or electromechanical frameworks, and its predictive capability is untested.

assumption_uncertainty.reason: Key assumptions—perfect impedance matching, linearity of pump response, and neglect of thermal effects—are highly speculative and unsupported by empirical evidence.

measurement_uncertainty.reason: Measurements reported are coarse, with no error bars or repeatability analysis, leading to moderate imprecision.

predictions.prediction: Age‑dependent stiffening of the ECM halves the perivascular CSF tracer influx velocity in mice.

predictions.falsification_threshold: If the mean increase is ≤10 % (≤0.55 kPa in seniors) the hypothesis is falsified.

predictions.falsification_threshold: If the half‑life reduction is ≤10 % (≤41 min) the hypothesis is falsified.

predictions.falsification_threshold: If the between‑group difference in SUVR change is <0.02, the hypothesis is falsified.

simulation.method: Hybrid finite-element / agent-based model with fluid-structure interaction (FSI) and poroelastic coupling. The perivascular CSF flow is solved using Biot's poroelasticity equations on a deformable tetrahedral mesh representing the brain parenchyma, with embedded 1D network elements for perivascular spaces. Cardiac and respiratory pulsations drive time-varying boundary conditions. Solute transport uses a coupled convection-diffusion-reaction solver with Lagrangian particle tracking for amyloid-beta oligomers and tau aggregates. ECM stiffening is parameterized via Darcy's permeability tensor and elastic modulus of the solid phase. Monte Carlo sampling handles inter-subject variability in arterial pulse waveforms and ECM composition.

classification.reasoning: The hypothesis combines several established concepts in a new way: (1) glymphatic clearance failure is known in aging and neurodegeneration, (2) brain ECM stiffening with age is documented, and (3) impedance matching/compliance gradients in fluid dynamics are established principles. However, the specific framing of glymphatic failure as primarily due to 'intrinsic pump function' loss via ECM stiffening and impaired impedance matching—rather than passive reduced clearance opportunity—represents a novel integration. The literature discusses glymphatic dysfunction and ECM changes separately, but does not formulate this specific mechanistic explanation linking ECM stiffening to pump efficiency via compliance gradient/impedance matching. The 'ECM Impedance-Matching Pump Theory' is a new conceptual framework, but it builds from known components rather than introducing an unknown mechanism.
